I have a speculation about where empirical distributions come from which has been a topic of personal rumination for me since the first year of my MSc thesis (*circa* 2020). It isn't scientific as far as I know, but it is the kind of thing that entertains me over a glass of beer.

The basic idea is to come up with a mathematical relationship between a hypothetical deterministic data generating process and empirical distributions. I'll focus on examples using differential equations.

## The Idea

The mechanism I have in mind has three ingredients, none of which is random by itself:

1. a deterministic trajectory $s(t)$ produced by a differential equation,
2. a *measurement schedule* — the times $t_1, t_2, \ldots$ at which we write down the state, and
3. an *observation map* — the part of the state we actually record. Observing only some of the state variables is precisely an [orthogonal projection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projection_(linear_algebra)#Orthogonal_projection) onto a coordinate subspace (followed, in practice, by whatever units conversion the instrument performs).

Record the projected values $P\, s(t_1), P\, s(t_2), \ldots$ and you have an empirical cumulative distribution function, regardless of how the trajectory was produced. So the question "where does the empirical distribution come from?" can be rephrased as: *which parts of the deterministic system, after projection and sampling, are responsible for the shape of that eCDF?* For [ergodic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodic_theory) systems there is a classical answer lurking: the time average along the trajectory converges to an average against the [invariant measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invariant_measure) of the system, so the histogram of samples converges to the pushforward of that invariant measure through the observation map. The empirical distribution is then not a property of the equations alone, nor of the projection alone, but of the pair.

The examples below are a catalogue of deterministic systems to think this through with. I have chosen a spread of behaviours — decay, oscillation, chaos, compartmental flow, switching — because the speculation is more interesting when the deterministic dynamics are varied.

## Van der Pol Oscillator

The [Van der Pol oscillator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_der_Pol_oscillator) is a non-conservative oscillator with non-linear damping.

$$\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = \mu (1 - x^2) \frac{dx}{dt} + x = 0$$


This can be written as a system of first-order differential equations:

$$\frac{dx}{dt} = y$$
$$\frac{dy}{dt} = \mu (1 - x^2) y - x$$

## Double Pendulum

A [double pendulum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_pendulum) exhibits complex dynamic behavior and is described by a system of second-order differential equations. Here I converted it to a system of first-order differential equations.

$$\frac{d\theta_1}{dt} = \omega_1$$
$$\frac{d\theta_2}{dt} = \omega_2$$
$$\frac{\omega_1}{dt} = \frac{-g(2m_1+m_2)\sin (\theta_1) - m_2 g \sin (\theta_1 - 2 \theta_2) - 2 \sin (\theta_1 - \theta_2) m_2 (\omega_2^2 L_2 + \omega_1^2 L_1 \cos (\theta_1 - \theta_2))}{L_1 (2m_1 + m_2 - m_2 \cos(2 \theta_1 - 2 \theta_2))}$$
$$\frac{d\omega_2}{dt} = \frac{2 \sin (\theta_1 - \theta_2) (\omega_1^2 L_1 (m_1 + m_2) + g(m_1 + m_2) \cos (\theta_1) + \omega_2^2 L_2 m_2 \cos (\theta_1 - \theta_2))}{L_2 (2 m_1 + m_2 - m_2 \cos (2 \theta_1 - 2 \theta_2))}$$

## SEIR Model (Epidemiology)

The [SEIR model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compartmental_models_in_epidemiology) is an extension of the SIR model, including an Exposed (E) compartment.

$$\frac{dS}{dt} = - \beta S I$$

$$\frac{dE}{dt} = \beta S I - \sigma E$$

$$\frac{dI}{dt} = \sigma E - \gamma I$$

$$\frac{dR}{dt} = \gamma I$$

## Chua's Circuit

[Chua's circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chua%27s_circuit) is a well-known example of a chaotic system. It is an electronic circuit that exhibits chaotic behavior and can be described by a system of three coupled nonlinear differential equations.

The equations for Chua's circuit are:

$$\frac{dx}{dt} = \alpha (y - x - h(x))$$
$$\frac{dy}{dt} = x - y + z$$
$$\frac{dz}{dt} = \beta z$$

where $h(x)$ is the piecewise linear function representing Chua's diode:

$$h(x) = m_1 x + \frac{1}{2} (m_0 - m_1) (|x+1| - |x- 1|)$$

## Reading the Catalogue

Each of the systems above produces, from entirely deterministic rules, trajectories whose sampled and projected values have recognisable distributions:

- Exponential decay gives a distribution of readings whose shape is dictated by how often you sample — sample uniformly in time and the eCDF of $x(t)$ is inherited from the decay curve directly.
- The oscillators (Van der Pol, Brusselator, FitzHugh-Nagumo, simple harmonic, Hodgkin-Huxley) spend their time near particular parts of a limit cycle, so a projected coordinate's histogram reflects the fraction of the cycle spent at each amplitude — slow sections pile up probability mass, fast sections shed it.
- The chaotic systems (Lorenz, Rössler, Chua, double pendulum) are the most striking cases: sensitive dependence makes individual trajectories unpredictable, yet the sampled values fill out a stable distribution-shaped object (the attractor's invariant measure, projected down). The distribution is *more* deterministic than the trajectory.
- The compartmental models (SIR, SEIR) produce readings whose distribution is shaped by the geometry of the flow between compartments and by when you chose to look.

In every case the empirical distribution is manufactured by the same three-part recipe: dynamics, schedule, projection. Change which coordinate you project onto and you get a different empirical distribution from the same system; change the schedule (e.g. sample once per period versus uniformly in time) and you get another. That sensitivity is, I think, the interesting part: the empirical distribution is not a hidden property waiting to be read off the differential equation, but a joint property of the system and the observation.

## Closing

I promised at the start that this speculation is not scientific as far as I know, and I will keep that promise: I have not derived a general result connecting a deterministic data generating process to the eCDF of its observations, and the ergodic-theory statement above only applies once you have already committed to a particular system and a stationary sampling scheme.

What the catalogue suggests to me is a modest rephrasing of the question I started with. Rather than asking where empirical distributions *come from*, it can be useful to ask which deterministic systems, sampled and projected in the ways we actually sample and project, would *reproduce* the empirical distribution in front of you. Sometimes the answer will be "no plausible deterministic story", which is itself informative. And sometimes — particularly with chaotic systems — the answer will be a deterministic system whose distribution is stable long before its trajectories are, which is the kind of situation that makes me reach for a beer and a fresh sheet of paper.
